DSA · Solved Past QuestionsLinked list II Q29 What is a linked list? Give the algorithm to create one with an example drawn graphically, and describe its types with diagrams.17th NTRCA CSE 2023 · BPSC AE 2022 · 18th NTRCA College ICT 2024 · singly, doubly, circular: BNPS AP 2017 102030NULL 1020 102030 singly: data | nextdoubly: prev | data | nextcircular: last → first struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; }; head = NULL; /* create 10 → 20 → 30 */ for each value x (taken in reverse: 30, 20, 10): n = malloc(sizeof *n); n->data = x; n->next = head; /* insert at front */ head = n; A linked list is a linear collection of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next; the list is reached through head and ends in NULL. Doubly lists also point back (easy reverse walk, delete given a node); circular lists link the last node to the first (round-robin queues). Q30 Can binary search be applied on a sorted linked list? Justify with an example.45th BCS CSE 2024Possible, but not efficient: finding the middle needs walking n/2 nodes, so total O(n), no better than linear search. On 3 → 8 → 15 → 21 → 34 the middle (15) costs 2 hops, the next middle 1 more… A skip list or BST gives O(log n). Q31 The list 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 is stored in sequence. Which of queue, heap, linked list, stack needs the least data movement to remove 11? Justify.38th BCS 2018Linked list: set 7's next to 13, nothing moves. Stack / queue must pop and push the others; an array shifts 13, 17; a heap re-heapifies. Q32 Can divide and conquer be applied to linked lists?bank IT viva Yes: merge sort is the natural sort for a linked list. Split at the middle with a slow and a fast pointer (O(n)), sort both halves, merge by relinking nodes: O(n log n) and no extra array. Binary search gains nothing, because reaching the middle already costs O(n). slow = head; fast = head->next; while (fast && fast->next) { slow = slow->next; fast = fast->next->next; } /* slow = end of first half */ 12
